curriculum.lessons.react-effects.title: Effects without the side effects
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.subtitl: Understand dependencies, cleanup, and the lifecycle of an effect.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.objecti: Synchronize a component with an external system without leaking connections or using stale values.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.concept: An effect synchronizes your component with something outside React: a connection, a browser event, or a timer. Derived values usually belong in render, and actions caused by a click usually belong in the event handler.

Every reactive value read by an effect belongs in its dependency list. React compares dependencies with Object.is. Before an effect re-runs with changed dependencies, React cleans up the previous effect; it also cleans up on unmount.
In development, Strict Mode runs an extra setup-and-cleanup cycle to help expose missing cleanup. Treat setup and cleanup as a matched pair, not as code that must run exactly once.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.scenari: A support dashboard switches between chat rooms. Each room needs a heartbeat timer. Changing rooms must stop the old timer so messages are never attributed to a room you left.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.mistake: Using [] while reading roomId leaves the timer with the initial room.
Suppressing the dependency linter hides stale closure bugs.
Omitting cleanup leaves timers running after the component unmounts.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.exercis: In your own React project, add this component and a button that switches roomId. Predict which room the next heartbeat will log, then verify it. Unmount the component and confirm that logging stops.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.questio: roomId changes from "general" to "support". What should happen?
Start a second timer alongside the first
Clear the old timer, then start a timer for support
Keep the old timer because the component is still mounted
The changed dependency causes cleanup of the previous effect before the next setup.
Why does an empty dependency array introduce a bug here?
Timers require an effect on every render
React never cleans up effects with empty dependencies
The timer callback keeps the initial roomId in its closure
With no dependency changes, the effect does not re-synchronize when roomId changes.
curriculum.lessons.react-effects.summary: Use effects for external synchronization. Declare reactive dependencies and make cleanup undo setup. Passing this check demonstrates concept recall, not hands-on React mastery.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.title: Make impossible states impossible
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.subtitle: Model an API request with discriminated unions.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.objectiv: Replace ambiguous optional fields with a union that TypeScript can narrow safely.
An object with loading, data, and error fields can represent contradictory combinations. A discriminated union gives each valid state a distinct literal tag.
Check the shared discriminant before accessing state-specific fields. TypeScript narrows the union within each branch. This is a compile-time guarantee; external JSON still needs runtime validation.
An exhaustive switch can use never to expose a missing branch when you add a new state. Avoid assertions that merely silence the compiler.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.scenario: A user profile panel must distinguish loading, success, and failure. It should never attempt to read a profile while loading.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.mistakes: Using data! bypasses the protection you need.
A TypeScript type does not validate a server response at runtime.
Independent booleans can encode loading and success simultaneously.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.exercise: Add an idle state and let the compiler identify the missing branch. Then write a small runtime guard that checks a received profile has a string name.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.question: What allows the compiler to safely access state.data?
Checking state.status === "success"
Casting state as Profile
Marking data optional on every state
The literal status value narrows the union to the member with a data field.
Does typing response.json() as Profile validate its contents?
Yes, TypeScript checks JSON automatically
No, incoming data still requires runtime validation
Only in strict mode
TypeScript types are erased at runtime. Validate untrusted data at the boundary.
curriculum.lessons.ts-narrowing.summary: Represent valid states explicitly. Narrow before accessing fields, and validate external input at runtime.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.title: Bring order to async work
curriculum.lessons.js-async.subtitle: Choose deliberate concurrency and handle failures.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.objective: Run independent operations concurrently while preserving result order and understanding rejection.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.concept.0: Awaiting each independent operation in a loop serializes the work. Mapping inputs to promises starts those operations before awaiting the combined result.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.concept.1: Promise.all returns results in input order, regardless of which operation completes first. It rejects when one input promise rejects; it does not cancel the other operations.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.concept.2: Use Promise.allSettled when you need every outcome. For large input sets, use a concurrency limit rather than starting thousands of requests at once.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.scenario: You need three independent account summaries for a dashboard. Start the reads together, but keep each result aligned with its original account ID.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.mistakes.0: forEach does not await an async callback.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.mistakes.1: Promise.all does not cancel pending requests on rejection.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.mistakes.2: Unbounded concurrency can overload a service or hit rate limits.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.exercise: Replace fetch with promises that resolve after different delays. Verify the result order. Make one reject, then compare Promise.all with Promise.allSettled.
The second request finishes first. Where is its result in Promise.all output?
Promise.all preserves the order of its inputs.
One promise rejects. What happens to the other requests?
They continue unless you explicitly cancel them
Aggregate rejection is not cancellation. AbortController can cancel compatible operations.
curriculum.lessons.js-async.summary: Match concurrency to dependencies. Preserve failure information and never assume rejection cancels work.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.title: The missing rows mystery
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.subtitle: Understand how filters change a LEFT JOIN.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.objective: Include parent records with no matching child rows while applying child filters correctly.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.concept.0: A LEFT JOIN retains each left-side row even when no right-side row matches. Missing right-side values are represented as NULL.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.concept.1: A WHERE condition on a right-side column can remove those unmatched rows. A comparison with NULL produces unknown, which does not pass WHERE.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.concept.2: To count only paid orders while retaining every customer, put the paid condition in ON and count a non-nullable order key, not COUNT(*).
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.scenario: A sales report must include customers with zero paid orders. Filtering status in WHERE accidentally removes those customers.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.mistakes.1: COUNT(*) counts the preserved customer row even when there is no order.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.mistakes.2: Joining multiple one-to-many tables can multiply rows before aggregation.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.exercise: Create two customers and one paid order for the first. Predict both result rows. Move the status filter to WHERE and explain which row disappears.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.questions.0: What does COUNT(orders.id) return for a customer with no paid orders?
COUNT(expression) ignores NULL values, so the unmatched row contributes zero.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.questions.1: Where should the paid-order filter live to retain every customer?
ON limits matches while LEFT JOIN still preserves the customer row.
curriculum.lessons.sql-joins.summary: Distinguish matching conditions from result filters. Count the child key when unmatched parents should contribute zero.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.title: Treat API failures as a contract
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.subtitle: Handle HTTP errors without hiding useful context.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.objective: Distinguish transport failures, HTTP errors, and invalid response bodies at an API boundary.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.concept.0: fetch rejects for some transport failures, but an HTTP 404 or 500 normally resolves to a Response. Check response.ok before treating a response as successful.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.concept.1: Reading JSON can fail even after a successful HTTP status. Runtime validation is a separate responsibility from parsing: valid JSON can still have the wrong shape.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.concept.2: Use stable, safe error messages at the UI boundary. Preserve diagnostic context for developers without exposing credentials or sensitive response bodies.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.scenario: An inventory view currently renders undefined after a 404. Give it a reliable contract: either return a valid quantity or throw a meaningful error.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.mistakes.0: Assuming a resolved fetch means HTTP success.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.mistakes.1: Treating parsed JSON as validated application data.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.mistakes.2: Retrying every failure, including permanent 400-level errors.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.exercise: List how the function behaves for a network failure, a 404, malformed JSON, a negative quantity, and a valid zero quantity. Decide which cases your UI should retry.
How does fetch usually handle a server response with status 500?
It resolves with a Response whose ok is false
HTTP error statuses still produce Response objects. The application checks the status.
Why check the quantity after parsing JSON?
Valid JSON can have an invalid domain shape or value
Syntax parsing does not enforce your domain contract.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.summary: Handle transport, HTTP, parsing, and domain failures as distinct cases. Keep the caller contract explicit.
curriculum.lessons.api-errors.next: Server-side validation and structured error responses
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.title: Undo safely. Keep the history.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.subtitle: Choose the right recovery tool for a shared branch.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.objectiv: Explain when to revert a shared commit and how to inspect history before recovery.
A revert creates a new commit that inverses the changes from an earlier commit. It preserves existing history, which makes it useful for changes already shared with teammates.
Reset moves a branch reference. The --hard option also overwrites the index and working tree, so it can discard uncommitted changes. Rewriting a published branch can disrupt collaborators.

Inspect status and history first. Use reflog to locate recent local reference movements when recovering a lost commit. Reflogs are local and have retention limits; they are not a substitute for backups.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.scenario: A small configuration change broke the shared main branch. You need a reviewable reversal that does not remove anyone else’s commits.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.mistakes: Using reset --hard before checking for uncommitted changes.
Force-pushing rewritten shared history without coordination.
Expecting revert to always be conflict-free.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.exercise: In a disposable repository, commit two small changes. Revert the first and inspect the new history. Explain why the original commit is still visible.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.question: What does git revert normally add to your branch?
Nothing; it deletes the old commit
A new commit that reverses an earlier change
A new remote repository
Revert records the inverse change in a new commit while retaining the existing history.
What is the main risk of reset --hard with uncommitted changes?
It deletes every remote branch
It disables reflog
It can overwrite uncommitted tracked-file changes
The hard mode resets the index and working tree, potentially discarding uncommitted work.
curriculum.lessons.git-recovery.summary: Inspect first. Prefer a reviewable revert for shared commits, and treat destructive local recovery with care.

challenges.challenges.group-transactions: Your reporting API receives transactions from several teams. Return an object mapping each category to its total amount. Keep negative refunds and do not mutate the input.
Export nothing: define a function named solve(transactions).
Each transaction has a category string and integer amount.
Treat unusual keys such as __proto__ as normal categories.
Return an empty object for an empty input.
You need one accumulator entry for each distinct category.
An object with no prototype avoids collisions with built-in property names.
Create Object.create(null); for each transaction, add its amount to the existing category total, defaulting to zero.

A single pass accumulates totals in O(n) time with O(k) space for k categories. A null-prototype object treats every category as data and avoids inherited properties. Using a Map and converting with Object.fromEntries is another valid approach.
challenges.challenges.merge-intervals.de: Merge overlapping or touching bookings represented by [start, end]. Return disjoint intervals sorted by start without changing the caller’s input.
challenges.challenges.merge-intervals.re: Define solve(intervals). Inputs are finite numeric intervals with start <= end.
Touching intervals such as [1,3] and [3,5] must merge.
challenges.challenges.merge-intervals.hi: Sort a copy of the intervals before deciding which overlap.
Compare each interval with the last interval in your output.
If current.start <= last.end, extend last.end to the larger end. Otherwise append a copy of current.
challenges.challenges.merge-intervals.ex: Sorting costs O(n log n). A linear scan then merges against the last emitted interval. Copying inner arrays avoids mutating the caller when extending an interval.
challenges.challenges.settled-results.de: A dashboard combines independent service operations. Each job descriptor has either a value or an error. Simulate each operation as a promise and return all outcomes in input order, including failures.
challenges.challenges.settled-results.re: Define async solve(jobs). For {value: x}, resolve x; for {error: message}, reject with that message.
One failure must not discard successful results.
challenges.challenges.settled-results.hi: Consider an aggregate promise utility that never discards other outcomes.
Promise.allSettled produces status, value, or reason for each operation.
Map descriptors into promises, await allSettled, then map each result into the required shape.
challenges.challenges.settled-results.ex: Promise.allSettled observes every operation and preserves order. Check presence of the error property instead of truthiness, because false, zero, and null are valid success values.
challenges.challenges.validate-form.desc: Validate a registration-shaped object without trusting its types. This exercise only validates data; no accounts are created.
challenges.challenges.validate-form.requ: Define solve(input), returning an ordered array of field names with invalid values.
name must be a string with at least two non-whitespace characters after trimming.
age must be an integer from 18 through 120 inclusive.
Check name before age. For null, arrays, or non-objects, both fields are invalid.
challenges.challenges.validate-form.hint: Check the shape of input before reading any fields.
typeof null is object; exclude null and arrays explicitly.
Use trim().length for name and Number.isInteger plus inclusive bounds for age.
challenges.challenges.validate-form.expl: Boundary validation separates parsing from domain rules. Do not coerce numeric strings into ages unless the API contract explicitly allows it.
challenges.challenges.bug-inventory.desc: A CSV importer supplies quantities as strings. The stock total sometimes becomes a long concatenated number. Find the root cause and return the numeric total.
challenges.challenges.bug-inventory.requ: Define solve(rows). Each row has quantity as a finite numeric string.
Do not mutate rows. Empty input should return 0.
challenges.challenges.bug-inventory.hint: Inspect the runtime type of both operands of +.
A TypeScript assertion does not convert a runtime value.
Convert the quantity at the boundary with Number before adding it.
challenges.challenges.bug-inventory.expl: The + operator concatenates when one operand is a string. Converting each quantity fixes the runtime behavior; a type assertion only hides the mismatch from TypeScript.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.title: A successful failure
challenges.challenges.bug-status.descrip: The API client marks failed HTTP responses as successful. Given a response-shaped object, classify it as {ok:true,data} for 2xx and {ok:false,status} otherwise.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.require: Define solve(response). HTTP status is an integer.
Every status from 200 through 299 is successful.
Preserve false, zero, and null data values on success.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.bug.act: The UI displays success for every nonzero status.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.hints.0: Truthiness is not an HTTP success check.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.hints.1: Check an inclusive lower bound and exclusive upper bound.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.hints.2: Success is status >= 200 && status < 300; do not use the truthiness of data either.
challenges.challenges.bug-status.explana: HTTP status codes are positive numbers, so checking truthiness accepts almost all responses. The success class is a numeric range.
challenges.challenges.bug-async.title: The results arrive after the return
challenges.challenges.bug-async.descript: An asynchronous transform returns an empty array before its work completes. Return the doubled numbers in their original order.
challenges.challenges.bug-async.requirem: Define async solve(values). The input is an array of finite numbers.
Use asynchronous transformations and wait for all results.
challenges.challenges.bug-async.hints.0: Does forEach return the promises from its callback?
challenges.challenges.bug-async.hints.1: Collect the promises using map instead.
challenges.challenges.bug-async.hints.2: Return await Promise.all(values.map(async value => ...)); each callback should return its own result.
challenges.challenges.bug-async.explanat: forEach discards callback return values. Awaiting forEach would not help. Map creates a promise array that Promise.all can await, preserving input order.
interviews.questions.fe-search.title: Search under pressure
interviews.questions.fe-search.prompt: A React search box fetches results after each keystroke. Older responses sometimes replace newer results. How would you fix it and test it?
interviews.questions.fe-search.signals.1: Cancel or ignore obsolete requests, including cleanup
interviews.questions.fe-search.signals.2: Test reversed response order and loading/error states
interviews.questions.fe-search.sample: I would key the request to the query, debounce only to reduce traffic, and abort the previous fetch in effect cleanup. I would also guard state updates with a request identity or an ignore flag because cancellation is not always supported. Abort errors should not become user-facing failures. A test should resolve the newest request first, then an older one, and assert that only the newest results remain. I would cover clearing the query and unmounting too.
interviews.questions.fe-dialog.title: An accessible dialog
interviews.questions.fe-dialog.prompt: Design an accessible confirmation dialog. Describe keyboard behavior, focus management, and what you would verify manually.
interviews.questions.fe-dialog.signals.0: Name the dialog and describe its semantics
interviews.questions.fe-dialog.signals.1: Manage initial focus, containment, Escape and restoration
interviews.questions.fe-dialog.sample: I would prefer a native dialog opened with showModal, give it an accessible name, and provide explicit cancel and confirm buttons. Initial focus should suit the action; a destructive action should not be the accidental default. Tab must stay within the modal, Escape should cancel, and closing should return focus to the trigger or a sensible fallback if it disappeared. I would test keyboard-only use, screen-reader announcements, zoom, and a long dialog on a small screen.
interviews.questions.fe-state.title: State ownership
interviews.questions.fe-state.prompt: A product list has filters, a selected item, and a filtered count. Which values would you store, derive, or put in the URL? Explain the tradeoffs.
interviews.questions.fe-state.sample: I would store the source list, filter inputs, and selected item ID, then derive the filtered list and count. Storing both the filtered list and count introduces synchronization bugs. Shareable filters belong in URL parameters with parsing and defaults; transient dialog state can stay local. I would lift shared state to the nearest common owner before adding a global store. Memoization is a performance choice after measurement, not a correctness requirement.
interviews.questions.be-retry.title: Safe retries
interviews.questions.be-retry.prompt: A client times out creating an order and retries. How do you prevent duplicate orders while allowing safe recovery?
interviews.questions.be-retry.signals.0: Use a client idempotency key with request fingerprint
interviews.questions.be-retry.signals.1: Make key reservation and order creation atomic
interviews.questions.be-retry.signals.2: Define concurrent retry and expiration behavior
interviews.questions.be-retry.sample: The client sends a stable idempotency key for the logical operation. The server records the key, caller, request fingerprint and result, using a unique constraint and a transaction with order creation. A retry with the same payload returns the stored result; reuse with a different payload is rejected. Concurrent requests must not both execute the side effect. External payments need their own idempotency support or an outbox workflow. I would document retention and test lost responses and simultaneous retries.
interviews.questions.be-auth.title: Object authorization
interviews.questions.be-auth.prompt: GET /invoices/:id authenticates the user but accepts any invoice ID. What could go wrong, and where should the fix live?
interviews.questions.be-auth.signals.1: Scope reads and writes to the caller or permitted organization
interviews.questions.be-auth.signals.2: Test cross-user access and avoid trusting client ownership fields
interviews.questions.be-auth.sample: Knowing who the caller is does not prove they can read an invoice. I would enforce ownership or organization membership on the server for every operation, ideally in the query itself. The organization must come from verified membership, not just a body parameter. Return a consistent forbidden or not-found response according to the information-disclosure policy. Tests should include two users, revoked membership, updates and deletes as well as reads.
interviews.questions.be-pagination.title: A changing feed
interviews.questions.be-pagination.promp: An activity feed is growing while users page through it. Compare offset and cursor pagination and propose an API.
interviews.questions.be-pagination.signa: Use a stable unique ordering and cursor
interviews.questions.be-pagination.sampl: Offsets are simple but inserts can shift later pages and large offsets may be expensive. I would sort by created_at and a unique ID, then encode both in an opaque cursor. The next query seeks after that pair using a matching index and a bounded page size. I would document whether the feed is a live view or a snapshot; cursors alone do not guarantee snapshot consistency. Tests include equal timestamps, new inserts, empty pages and malformed cursors.
interviews.questions.fs-optimistic.title: Optimistic updates
interviews.questions.fs-optimistic.promp: A task board immediately moves a card before the server responds. How do you handle failure and conflicting edits from another user?
interviews.questions.fs-optimistic.signa: Track pending state and preserve a recovery path
Use versions or another concurrency policy
interviews.questions.fs-optimistic.sampl: I would keep the previous position and mark the move pending. The request includes the version the client edited; a conditional update detects conflicts. On failure I can restore the old position if no newer local edit superseded it, otherwise refetch and reconcile. A conflict should show the current server state and let the user retry deliberately. Request IDs prevent old responses overwriting newer moves. I would test reordered responses and two clients moving the same card.
interviews.questions.fs-upload.title: File upload pipeline
interviews.questions.fs-upload.prompt: Design a profile-image upload flow from browser to storage. Cover validation, authorization and what happens if upload succeeds but saving the profile fails.
interviews.questions.fs-upload.signals.0: Validate server-side and scope upload permissions
interviews.questions.fs-upload.signals.1: Separate temporary upload from committed reference
interviews.questions.fs-upload.sample: The server authorizes an upload and issues a short-lived, object-scoped destination. Client validation helps usability, but the server must verify size and actual content, generate safe names and restrict serving behavior. I would upload to a temporary object, then commit the verified object reference to the profile. Failed commits leave an orphan cleaned up by an expiry job. The UI should show progress and retry without claiming the profile changed until confirmation arrives.
interviews.questions.fs-contract.title: An evolving API
interviews.questions.fs-contract.prompt: A frontend and backend deploy independently. A new required address field is being introduced. How would you roll out the change without breaking old clients?
interviews.questions.fs-contract.sample: I would first add server support with a compatible default or optional field and migrate stored records where possible. Then deploy a client that sends the new field and handles both response shapes. Runtime validation is still necessary even with shared TypeScript types. After measuring old-client usage and establishing a supported-version policy, I would enforce the requirement, possibly in a new API version. Contract tests should cover both old and new clients during the transition.
interviews.questions.db-index.title: Choosing an index
interviews.questions.db-index.prompt: Orders are queried by customer_id, sorted by created_at descending, with LIMIT 20. What index would you consider, and how would you verify it helps?
interviews.questions.db-index.signals.0: Match equality filtering and ordered access
interviews.questions.db-index.signals.1: Inspect the execution plan with realistic data
interviews.questions.db-index.signals.2: Account for index write and storage costs
interviews.questions.db-index.sample: I would consider a composite index starting with customer_id followed by created_at, and an ID tie-breaker if pagination requires stable ordering. I would inspect the query plan and measured execution with representative cardinalities, checking examined rows and whether sorting is avoided. An index is not free: it uses storage and increases write work. I would compare before and after under realistic workloads rather than assuming every sequential scan is wrong.
interviews.questions.db-transfer.title: Concurrent transfers
interviews.questions.db-transfer.prompt: Two requests transfer money from the same account. Explain how you would preserve the balance invariant and avoid partial transfers.
interviews.questions.db-transfer.signals: Debit and credit in one transaction
Protect the balance check against concurrent changes
Use exact monetary representation and test rollback
interviews.questions.db-transfer.sample: I would use integer minor units or a suitable exact decimal, never binary floating point for money. Within one transaction, I would lock the affected rows in a deterministic order or use a conditional debit that succeeds only with sufficient funds, then credit the recipient and write the ledger. A failed step rolls back all changes. Constraints provide another line of defense. I would test simultaneous withdrawals, deadlock retries, insufficient funds and failure after the debit.
interviews.questions.db-join.title: Customers with no orders
interviews.questions.db-join.prompt: Write or describe a query returning every customer and the count of their orders, including customers with zero orders. What common mistake hides those customers?
interviews.questions.db-join.signals.0: Use LEFT JOIN and count the non-null order key
interviews.questions.db-join.signals.2: Group correctly and cover zero/multiple orders
interviews.questions.db-join.sample: SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id returns zero for unmatched customers. COUNT(*) would count the unmatched left row as one. A filter such as o.status = completed in WHERE removes unmatched customers; if the goal is completed-order counts while keeping all customers, put that filter in the join condition. I would test customers with zero, one, and several qualifying orders.
interviews.questions.net-async.title: Async request handling
interviews.questions.net-async.prompt: An ASP.NET request handler calls an async database method using .Result. Why is that a problem, and how would you propagate cancellation?
interviews.questions.net-async.signals.1: Use await through the call chain
interviews.questions.net-async.signals.2: Pass request cancellation and handle it appropriately
interviews.questions.net-async.sample: Calling .Result blocks a request thread while I/O is pending and can contribute to thread-pool starvation under load. In environments with a captured synchronization context it can also deadlock, though that is not the usual ASP.NET Core context. I would make the handler async, await the operation, and pass the request CancellationToken into database and HTTP calls. Cancellation is cooperative; I would avoid reporting expected client cancellation as an internal server error.
interviews.questions.net-di.title: Dependency lifetimes
interviews.questions.net-di.prompt: A singleton service captures a scoped database context. Explain the issue and propose a design for a background job that needs database access.
interviews.questions.net-di.signals.0: Identify captive dependency and context concurrency risk
interviews.questions.net-di.signals.1: Create and dispose an explicit scope or context per unit of work
interviews.questions.net-di.signals.2: Avoid sharing one context across parallel jobs
interviews.questions.net-di.sample: The singleton outlives the request scope and must not capture its context. A database context is a unit-of-work object and should not be shared across concurrent operations. For a background job I would create a scope through a scope factory, resolve the scoped service within it, await the work and dispose the scope. A context factory can also create independent contexts per job. I would test repeated and concurrent jobs and ensure cancellation and disposal work.
interviews.questions.net-query.title: Query boundaries
interviews.questions.net-query.prompt: A repository calls ToList before filtering a large table. Explain the impact and how you would shape a read-only query.
interviews.questions.net-query.signals.0: Distinguish server query composition from in-memory enumeration
interviews.questions.net-query.signals.1: Project only needed fields and bound results
interviews.questions.net-query.signals.2: Inspect generated SQL and avoid N+1 queries
interviews.questions.net-query.sample: Materializing first moves all rows into application memory and makes later filtering run locally. I would compose the supported Where, ordering, projection and pagination before materialization, then await the database call. For read-only entity results, disabling tracking can reduce overhead. I would inspect generated SQL and watch for N+1 access to related data. Not every .NET expression translates to SQL, so translation and performance need verification against the actual provider.
interviews.questions.js-loop.title: Event loop ordering
interviews.questions.js-loop.prompt: What is logged by: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D");? Explain why.
interviews.questions.js-loop.signals.1: Distinguish synchronous stack, microtasks and timer task
interviews.questions.js-loop.signals.2: Explain that zero delay is not immediate execution
interviews.questions.js-loop.sample: The order is A, D, C, B. The current script runs synchronously through A and D. The resolved promise schedules a microtask that runs after the stack is empty and before the next timer task. The zero-delay timer makes B eligible for a later task; it does not interrupt the current script. Long synchronous work can delay both callbacks, and a continuously replenished microtask queue can delay tasks too.
interviews.questions.js-closure.title: Closures and loops
interviews.questions.js-closure.prompt: Why do callbacks created in a for(var i = 0; i < 3; i++) loop often print 3 three times when invoked later? Give two fixes.
Use per-iteration let binding or a function parameter
Distinguish captured binding from a frozen value
interviews.questions.js-closure.sample: Each callback closes over the same var binding, not a snapshot of its value. After the loop, that binding contains 3. Using let in the loop creates a distinct binding for each iteration, so the callbacks observe 0, 1 and 2. Alternatively, pass i into a helper that returns a callback; each invocation has its own parameter binding. I would test invoking the callbacks after the loop rather than only during it.
interviews.questions.js-parallel.title: Parallel requests
interviews.questions.js-parallel.prompt: A dashboard loads three independent widgets. Compare sequential await, Promise.all and Promise.allSettled, including failure and cancellation behavior.
interviews.questions.js-parallel.signals: Describe latency and aggregate failure differences
Choose behavior based on partial rendering needs
Do not assume rejection cancels other work
interviews.questions.js-parallel.sample: Sequential await starts the next request only after the previous completes, increasing total latency for independent work. Starting all requests and awaiting Promise.all allows concurrency but rejects if any input rejects. Promise.allSettled lets each widget render a success or an error independently. Neither aggregate automatically cancels other requests when one fails; cancellation needs explicit support such as AbortController. I would also bound concurrency when the number of widgets is large.
interviews.questions.debug-race.title: A stale counter
interviews.questions.debug-race.prompt: A React click handler calls setCount(count + 1) three times but the counter increases once. Diagnose it and describe a regression test.
Explain render snapshot and queued replacement values
Use functional updates for dependent transitions
Test observable behavior instead of implementation calls
interviews.questions.debug-race.sample: All three expressions read the same count from that render, so they queue the same replacement value. If three increments are intended, use setCount(c => c + 1) three times or one functional increment by three. Each updater then receives the preceding queued result. A regression test clicks once and checks that the displayed count increases by three, including from a nonzero starting state. I would avoid testing the number of setter calls.
interviews.questions.debug-latency.title: A slow endpoint
interviews.questions.debug-latency.promp: An endpoint went from 100 ms to 2 seconds after a release. How would you investigate before changing code?
interviews.questions.debug-latency.signa: Compare percentiles, traffic and release changes
Use traces to separate database, external I/O and CPU time
Form and test a hypothesis, then verify the fix
interviews.questions.debug-latency.sampl: I would confirm the regression using latency percentiles, error rate, traffic and a deployment timeline. A representative trace can show whether time is in database queries, an external dependency, queueing or application code. I would compare query counts and plans, payload sizes and configuration with the previous release. Then I would reproduce a narrow hypothesis with realistic data, apply the smallest fix or rollback, and compare the same measurements under similar load.
interviews.questions.debug-leak.title: Growing memory
interviews.questions.debug-leak.prompt: A page becomes slower after opening and closing a live preview repeatedly. What evidence would you collect and what lifecycle bugs would you inspect?
Inspect retained objects and active resources
Pair subscription setup with cleanup and verify recovery
interviews.questions.debug-leak.sample: I would repeat the same open/close sequence and compare memory after garbage collection rather than treating every peak as a leak. Heap snapshots and allocation profiles can reveal retained listeners, closures or detached DOM nodes. I would inspect timers, event subscriptions, observers and socket handlers created by the preview, ensuring cleanup uses the same callback identity and closes resources. Then I would repeat the sequence and verify that retained memory and active subscriptions stabilize.
interviews.questions.behavior-conflict.p: Tell me about a disagreement over a technical approach. What did you do personally, how was the decision made, and what would you change?
interviews.questions.behavior-conflict.s: Describe a specific situation and your own actions
State an honest outcome and reflection

Example structure, not a story to claim as your own: Our team disagreed about adding a cache before a release. I asked what latency target we needed, measured the slow query and compared a query fix with cache invalidation complexity. We agreed on the query fix and a follow-up threshold for caching. I would report the actual measured outcome and explain what I learned about involving operations earlier. If you have no work example, use an honest study or personal-project example.
interviews.questions.behavior-incident.p: Describe a bug you introduced. How did you discover it, communicate the impact, recover, and prevent recurrence?
interviews.questions.behavior-incident.s: Own a concrete contribution without blaming others

Use a real example and separate your actions from the team’s. A useful structure is: I changed a parser and missed an empty-input case; a support report exposed it. I confirmed the affected paths, told the team what was known, and helped roll back before investigating fully. I then added a regression case and clarified the input contract in review. State the real impact and outcome; do not invent incident numbers or claim that one test prevents all future mistakes.
You are asked to “make onboarding better” by next week. How would you turn that into a deliverable and communicate uncertainty?
Clarify the user problem and success measure
Agree on feedback and report actual results

I would ask which users struggle and examine the evidence: support feedback, completion data or a walkthrough. I would agree on one measurable problem, such as a confusing required field, and choose a small change that fits the week. I would document assumptions and dependencies, show a quick prototype early, and define how we will evaluate it. At the end I would distinguish what shipped from what the evidence shows, including if the sample is too small to establish improvement.
projects.projects.reading-queue.title: A thoughtful reading queue
projects.projects.reading-queue.tasks.0: Define an Article type with a stable ID, title, URL and read flag.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tasks.1: Build a labeled add form with inline validation and a keyboard-friendly list.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tasks.2: Add unread/all filters and derive the visible count from source data.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tasks.3: Persist a versioned collection and handle invalid saved data without silently replacing it.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tasks.4: Write interaction tests and a README explaining setup and storage limitations.
projects.projects.reading-queue.acceptan: Blank titles and non-HTTP(S) URLs are rejected with specific messages.
Adding, marking read and removing one item never changes another item.
Filters and visible counts stay consistent after every edit.
Reload restores the queue; a failed write is visible and does not claim success.
Every action is available by keyboard and the empty queue explains how to begin.
projects.projects.reading-queue.architec: Keep the article collection in one owner; derive filtering and counts.
Use pure add/update/remove functions with IDs rather than array indexes.
Put parsing and storage behind a small repository boundary. Keep form draft state separate from persisted articles.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tests.0: Add two identical titles with different URLs, delete one and verify the other remains.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tests.1: Enter whitespace, javascript: and malformed URLs; verify no item is added.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tests.2: Mark the last unread item as read while filtering unread; verify the empty state and count.
projects.projects.reading-queue.tests.3: Seed malformed JSON and simulate a quota error; verify visible recovery without a silent reset.
projects.projects.reading-queue.hints.0: Sketch the state first: articles plus a filter value. Avoid a second stored filteredArticles array.
projects.projects.reading-queue.hints.1: Use new URL for parsing, then explicitly allow only http: and https:. A stable ID distinguishes duplicate titles.
projects.projects.reading-queue.hints.2: Inject a storage adapter in tests. Parse unknown data before using it; retain in-memory edits when a write fails.
projects.projects.issue-api.title: A dependable issue API
projects.projects.issue-api.tasks.0: Write the request/response contract, allowed statuses and error shape.
projects.projects.issue-api.tasks.1: Create a migration for issues with required fields and constraints.
projects.projects.issue-api.tasks.2: Implement CRUD endpoints with boundary validation and parameterized queries.
projects.projects.issue-api.tasks.3: Add bounded pagination, deterministic ordering and status filters.
projects.projects.issue-api.tasks.4: Write API integration tests against an isolated database and document example requests.
projects.projects.issue-api.acceptance.0: Invalid titles, statuses, IDs and page sizes return documented client errors.
projects.projects.issue-api.acceptance.1: Unknown IDs return a consistent not-found response.
projects.projects.issue-api.acceptance.2: List ordering includes a unique tie-breaker and pages obey the requested bound.
projects.projects.issue-api.acceptance.3: Only supplied, permitted fields change in an update; SQL input remains data.
projects.projects.issue-api.acceptance.4: Database failures produce a controlled response without leaking internals.
projects.projects.issue-api.architecture: Separate HTTP parsing, issue service rules and database operations.
Use a migration-managed relational table and parameterized queries.
Give tests a disposable database and deterministic fixtures; do not use production data.
projects.projects.issue-api.tests.0: Create, fetch, update and delete an issue; verify the deleted record is not returned.
projects.projects.issue-api.tests.1: Try an unknown status, blank title and injection-like title; verify validation or literal storage.
projects.projects.issue-api.tests.2: Insert several rows with equal timestamps and verify stable pagination.
projects.projects.issue-api.tests.3: Force a repository error and verify the public error body excludes connection strings and SQL.
projects.projects.issue-api.hints.0: Start with a table of routes, valid input and response statuses before writing handlers.
projects.projects.issue-api.hints.1: Validate a patch using an explicit allowlist. Build queries from fixed SQL and bound values.
projects.projects.issue-api.hints.2: Choose an ordering such as created_at plus id. Test two consecutive pages against a fixture with tied timestamps.
projects.projects.booking-board.title: A conflict-aware booking board
projects.projects.booking-board.tasks.0: Define room, booking and owner records with a documented time-zone policy.
projects.projects.booking-board.tasks.1: Build a form and day view with loading, empty, pending and conflict states.
projects.projects.booking-board.tasks.2: Enforce ownership and overlap rules on the server.
projects.projects.booking-board.tasks.3: Protect concurrent booking creation with database constraints or an appropriate locking transaction.
projects.projects.booking-board.tasks.4: Add concurrent-request tests and document local setup and the identity model.
projects.projects.booking-board.acceptan: End time must be after start time; invalid or ambiguous times are handled explicitly.
Overlapping bookings for one room are rejected even under concurrent requests.
Adjacent intervals are allowed under a documented half-open interval policy.
A user cannot cancel another user’s booking by guessing its ID.
Conflicts show a useful message and refresh availability without claiming a booking succeeded.
projects.projects.booking-board.architec: Use a React form and day view backed by a server-owned booking service.
Store unambiguous instants and present them in the selected room time zone.
Enforce overlap inside the database transaction, not solely with a client-side availability check.
projects.projects.booking-board.tests.0: Submit two overlapping bookings concurrently; assert exactly one succeeds.
projects.projects.booking-board.tests.2: Try cancelling another owner’s booking and confirm it remains.
projects.projects.booking-board.tests.3: Simulate a slow response, server rejection and a daylight-saving boundary; check both data and messages.
projects.projects.booking-board.hints.0: Two intervals overlap when startA < endB and startB < endA for half-open intervals.
projects.projects.booking-board.hints.1: A check followed by an insert can race. Consider an exclusion constraint, or serialize booking changes by locking the room row.
projects.projects.booking-board.hints.2: Send machine-readable timestamps with offsets. Display the room’s zone and test conversion separately from the overlap rule.
projects.projects.sales-report.title: A trustworthy sales report
projects.projects.sales-report.tasks.0: Model customers, orders and order lines with foreign keys and exact monetary values.
projects.projects.sales-report.tasks.1: Seed zero-order customers, multi-line orders, cancelled orders and month-boundary dates.
projects.projects.sales-report.tasks.2: Write customer counts including zero and monthly completed-order revenue.
projects.projects.sales-report.tasks.3: Define time-zone, currency and refund assumptions explicitly.
projects.projects.sales-report.tasks.4: Inspect query plans, add a justified index and write expected-result checks.
projects.projects.sales-report.acceptanc: Customers without orders appear with count zero.
An order with multiple lines is counted once in order-count reports.
Revenue excludes cancelled orders and does not mix currencies without an explicit conversion policy.
Month boundaries follow the documented reporting zone and use exact arithmetic.
Expected totals can be independently calculated from a small seed fixture.
projects.projects.sales-report.architect: Separate transactional schema, seed fixtures and reporting queries.
Aggregate each one-to-many relation at the intended grain before joining summaries.
Keep schema changes in migrations and explain each index with a query plan.
projects.projects.sales-report.tests.0: One customer, two orders and three lines in each order must still produce order count two.
projects.projects.sales-report.tests.1: A customer with no orders must appear with zero, not disappear through a WHERE filter.
projects.projects.sales-report.tests.2: Place orders just before and after a reporting-month boundary and verify bucket placement.
projects.projects.sales-report.tests.3: Mix completed, cancelled and refunded fixtures; verify the documented revenue policy exactly.
projects.projects.sales-report.hints.0: Write the grain of every result in plain language: one row per customer or one row per month and currency.
projects.projects.sales-report.hints.1: Use LEFT JOIN for zero-order customers and count a nullable child key, not COUNT(*).
projects.projects.sales-report.hints.2: Pre-aggregate line totals per order before joining to customer summaries. Compare against hand-calculated fixture totals.
projects.projects.inventory-dotnet.title: An inventory reservation service
projects.projects.inventory-dotnet.tasks: Model stock and reservations with quantity constraints and unique operation keys.
Create async reserve and release endpoints with validation and cancellation tokens.
Perform stock updates and reservation writes in a single transaction.
Make duplicate operations idempotent and release a reservation at most once.
Add concurrency and rollback integration tests and document the endpoint contract.
projects.projects.inventory-dotnet.accep: Zero, negative and non-integral quantities are rejected.
Concurrent reservations never reserve more units than available.
Retrying the same operation key and payload returns the existing result; changed payloads are rejected.
Releasing twice restores stock only once.
Failure after a stock update rolls back both stock and reservation changes.
projects.projects.inventory-dotnet.archi: Keep HTTP handlers thin and use a scoped reservation service and database context.
Use conditional updates or locking in a transaction to enforce stock invariants.
Give operation keys a unique constraint and bind them to the caller and request fingerprint.
projects.projects.inventory-dotnet.tests: With five units left, submit two concurrent requests for four; only one can succeed.
Send the same operation key twice and assert exactly one reservation and one deduction.
Release the same reservation concurrently and assert stock is restored once.
Inject a failure between stock mutation and reservation insert; assert the original balance remains.
projects.projects.inventory-dotnet.hints: Write invariants before endpoints: available >= 0, one reservation per operation key, one release per reservation.
An UPDATE with a sufficient-stock predicate can atomically claim inventory; inspect the affected-row count.
Keep the stock mutation and reservation insert in the same transaction. Handle unique-key conflicts as retries only when the request fingerprint matches.
projects.projects.resilient-search.title: A resilient search explorer
projects.projects.resilient-search.tasks: Create a deterministic mock API with data, delayed responses and a failure mode.
Build query, loading, results, empty and error states.
Prevent obsolete requests from replacing current results and clean up on unmount.
Add an explicit retry action and keyboard-accessible result navigation.
Write race-condition tests and document the original bug, fix and remaining tradeoffs.
projects.projects.resilient-search.accep: Rapidly changing the query always leaves results for the latest query.
Clearing the query clears obsolete results and prevents pending responses from restoring them.
A failed request shows a retry action that actually repeats the current query.
Aborted obsolete requests do not show an error for the current query.
A user can search, navigate results and retry with only the keyboard.
projects.projects.resilient-search.archi: Keep the mock transport separate from the search-state hook and presentation.
Track a request identity or cleanup flag in addition to any supported cancellation.
Treat debounce as a traffic optimization and stale-response protection as a separate correctness rule.
projects.projects.resilient-search.tests: Resolve a newer query first and an older query second; assert only the newer results are visible.
Clear the input during a request, then resolve it; assert the initial state remains.
Fail one request then retry successfully; assert the error is replaced by current results.
Unmount while loading and verify listener, timer and request cleanup.
projects.projects.resilient-search.hints: List the allowed state transitions before implementing the hook. Distinguish no query from no matches.
Debouncing alone cannot stop an old response arriving late. Compare request identity before committing results.
Use deferred promises in tests so you control resolution order without relying on real time or a network.
assessment.diagnostics.react.react-place: A component displays fullName from firstName and lastName props. Where should it calculate fullName?
In an effect that updates another state variable
During render from the current props
A value derived entirely from current props can be calculated during render. No external system needs synchronization.
assessment.diagnostics.react.react-depen: An effect opens a connection using the roomId prop. Which dependency list keeps the connection synchronized when roomId changes?
No changes are needed if the component stays mounted
roomId is a reactive value read by the effect. Including it lets React reconnect when the room changes.
assessment.diagnostics.react.react-clean: An effect starts an interval. What should its returned cleanup function do?
Clear the interval created by that setup
Cleanup undoes setup. Clearing that interval prevents it from continuing after unmount or after the effect is replaced.
assessment.diagnostics.javascript.js-con: Three independent reads should start together. Which approach does that?
Await each read inside a for loop
Start reads with map, then await Promise.all
Use forEach and await its return value
Mapping to promises starts the independent reads before awaiting their combined result. A loop that awaits each read serializes them.
assessment.diagnostics.javascript.js-ord: Promise.all([slowRead, fastRead]) succeeds. Which result is first?
Promise.all preserves input order even when operations finish in a different order.
assessment.diagnostics.javascript.js-rej: One input to Promise.all rejects while another request is pending. What happens?
The pending request is automatically cancelled
The aggregate resolves with partial results
The aggregate rejects; the pending request continues unless explicitly cancelled
Aggregate rejection does not cancel other work. Cancellation requires a separate mechanism supported by the operation.
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-left.prom: Customers LEFT JOIN orders has a customer with no matching orders. What does the join produce for that customer?
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-left.opti: A row with NULL order columns
A row with an invented order ID of zero
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-left.expl: LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched left-side rows and fills the right-side columns with NULL.
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-filter.pr: A report must retain every customer but join only paid orders. Where should orders.status = 'paid' go?
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-filter.op: In WHERE after the LEFT JOIN
In the LEFT JOIN ON condition
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-filter.ex: Filtering matches in ON retains customers with no paid orders. A WHERE comparison on the missing order removes their NULL-extended rows.
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-count.pro: After a LEFT JOIN, which expression counts zero for a customer with no orders, assuming orders.id is a non-null primary key?
assessment.diagnostics.sql.sql-count.exp: COUNT(expression) ignores NULL, so COUNT(orders.id) counts only matched orders. COUNT(*) includes the preserved customer row.
assessment.diagnostics.node.node-http.pr: A fetch request receives an HTTP 500 response. What normally happens?
assessment.diagnostics.node.node-http.ex: HTTP error responses normally resolve to a Response. Check response.ok or status explicitly; transport failures can reject.
assessment.diagnostics.node.node-body.pr: An HTTP 200 response parses as { quantity: -2 }. The contract requires a non-negative integer. What should the client do?
assessment.diagnostics.node.node-body.op: Accept it because the HTTP status is 200
assessment.diagnostics.node.node-body.ex: HTTP success and JSON syntax do not validate the domain. Check the quantity type, integer constraint, and allowed range.
assessment.diagnostics.node.node-boundar: An upstream failure contains internal debug details. What should a public API expose?
A stable, safe error message, while retaining appropriate diagnostic context internally
Credentials so the caller can debug
Public error contracts should be useful without exposing credentials or sensitive internals. Keep appropriate diagnostic context at the developer boundary.
assessment.diagnostics.git.git-shared.pr: A commit on a shared branch needs to be undone while preserving history. Which operation normally fits?
assessment.diagnostics.git.git-shared.op: Revert the commit with a new inverse commit
assessment.diagnostics.git.git-shared.ex: Revert records an inverse change as a new commit, preserving the history collaborators already have.
Why inspect git status before considering git reset --hard?
Hard reset automatically backs up every change
Hard reset can discard uncommitted tracked-file changes
Hard reset updates the index and working tree. Inspect and protect uncommitted work before any destructive recovery.
assessment.diagnostics.git.git-reflog.pr: A local branch was moved and a recent commit seems lost. What can help locate its previous tip?
assessment.diagnostics.git.git-reflog.op: The local reflog, subject to retention limits
A guarantee that git status lists all deleted commits
assessment.diagnostics.git.git-reflog.ex: Reflog records recent local reference movements and can help locate a lost commit. It is local, expires, and is not a backup.
